title: Your first report
subtitle: A real analysis: from someone else's complaint to a number you can defend in a meeting

units.title: Frame the problem
units.subtitle: How to turn someone else's complaint into a question that can be answered

lessons.title: A question that can be answered
lessons.summary: A complaint is not a task. A task is a decision, a deadline and a constraint

cards.heading: What we are going to do
cards.text:
The whole course is built around one real-world problem at a distributor called Delta. You play an analyst in your first weeks on the job: the same data extract, the same colleagues with questions and the same deadline, next Tuesday. By the end you will have a report on the platform and an answer you can state calmly in a meeting.

Here is the problem. Over the quarter, sales grew by 4%. At the same time, expiry write-offs grew by 31%, and “out of stock on the shelf” complaints doubled. What is going on, and what should be done about it?
list: break down someone else's complaint into a question that has an answer;
get a report from the model and upload it to the platform;
check the data extract and find six things in it that change the conclusion;
fix the report and publish a second version;
write five lines to your manager that lead to someone making a decision.
cards.note: You will do the calculations yourself, and that is the point: something you found with your own hands sounds different in a meeting. Pick your tool: Excel or queries on the platform; both paths are laid out step by step. If your numbers do not match, a separate lesson shows how to find where they diverge. About two hours in total; one lesson a day works fine.

cast.say: Sales are up, yet the shelves are empty. Get to the bottom of it by Tuesday.

cards.text:
Delta buys bottled drinks from a manufacturer: water in two sizes, 0.5 and 1.5 liters, lemonade and iced tea. Four items, and that is exactly what they are called in the extract. It delivers them to sixty stores in three cities. The stores differ: supermarkets, convenience stores and petrol stations. Once a week the warehouse collects a batch from the manufacturer, and once a week a truck makes the round of the stores. Two actions and two levers: how much to buy in total, and how to split what was bought across stores.

Over the quarter, sales grew by 4%. At the same time, expiry write-offs grew by 31%, and “out of stock on the shelf” complaints doubled.

cards.heading: What you have to work with
cards.text:
The analyst was given a twelve-week extract from the accounting system: an Excel workbook with two sheets. The main sheet, Sales, has one row per store, per item, per day.

The second sheet, Warehouse, is shorter: what the warehouse shipped to each store on delivery day, and at what price. You will need it for reconciliation: sales and shipments should match, and wherever they do not, that is usually where the explanation hides.

Here it is. Download it and take a look inside right now. We will keep coming back to it throughout the course, and it helps if by then you have already seen what it looks like. No Excel? Use the same sheets as plain files: delta-sales.csv for sales, delta-stock.csv for the warehouse.
list: sold that day, in units;
delivered that day: how much the truck dropped off;
written off at expiry;
stock at the end of the day.
cards.note: Neither the growth in sales nor the growth in write-offs is visible in this extract. It covers twelve weeks day by day, and the previous quarter is not there at all, so there is nothing to compare against. This happens a lot: part of what you are told cannot be checked. That is fine. What is not fine is not knowing which part.

cards.heading: Two problems at once is a clue
cards.text:
Write-offs mean that some stores have more product than they can sell. Empty shelves mean that others have less than customers want to buy. Each problem on its own is fixed by purchasing: buy more or less from the manufacturer.

But both grew at once. So the total we buy is roughly right; what is wrong is how that volume is split across stores. That conclusion is reached before the file is even opened.

This gives a task you can actually start on: revise the per-store delivery quota for next week without changing the purchase from the manufacturer. Such a decision costs nothing: the total volume stays the same, only its distribution changes.

cards.heading: What the task must make clear
cards.text: Before calculating anything, test the brief against four points. If even one is missing, go back to whoever brought you the task and ask. This is not nitpicking: without these four things you will still produce a report, but it will be of no use.
list: What decision the answer drives: how much product to send to each store.
By when: in time for next Tuesday's delivery.
What is off limits: buying more from the manufacturer.
What result would make the answer useless: if no store has a surplus, there is nothing to redistribute.
cards.note: If the task does not say what decision the report will inform, the work never ends. Any table will do, and none of them will help.

checks.q: Here are four ways to phrase the same task. Which one makes clear what to do and when the work is finished?
options: Analyze the trend in sales and write-offs over the last quarter
Find out why the company's product write-offs are increasing
By Tuesday, revise the delivery quota without raising purchases
Put together a summary of all stores broken down by channel
checks.why: It states what is being decided (the delivery quota), by when (Tuesday) and what is off limits (raising purchases). A task like this tells you when to stop. The other three do not say what result counts as done: you could keep building tables against them forever.

lessons.title: The issue tree
lessons.summary: Break the problem down so the branches do not overlap and together cover everything

cards.heading: Four branches
cards.text: Before calculating, break the question “why are shortages and write-offs growing together” into non-overlapping causes. There should be only a few, and together they must cover everything.
list: Purchases are too small: the total volume is not enough for the whole network.
Volume goes to the wrong stores: a surplus in some places, a shortage in others.
Volume goes to the wrong items within a store: the assortment is off.
The data is wrong: the extract is flawed, and so is every conclusion drawn from it.

cards.text:
The fourth branch is not a technical formality before the real work starts; it is a cause in its own right. Until it is closed, the first three are worth nothing: you will be explaining to the business things that never happened.

That is exactly why it is checked first. At Delta, the extract turned out to contain a duplicated week, two cities using different units of measure, and a store with blanks instead of numbers. Any conclusion drawn before that clean-up would have been wrong, and convincing.

cards.heading: One number closes a branch
cards.text:
The first branch is the quickest to rule out. Over twelve weeks the warehouse shipped 1,817,738 bottles to stores, while estimated demand was 1,762,387. In other words, 3.1% more reached the shelves than customers were ready to take.

In total there is enough product. A quarter of the work fell away after a single comparison, and the question left is not “how much to buy” but “how to split it across stores”.
cards.note: If a single number closes a branch, calculate it first. At Delta, comparing shipments with demand took a minute and removed a whole branch from the work: purchase volume no longer needed any thought.

cards.heading: Store or item
cards.text:
The two middle branches are easy to confuse, yet they lead to different decisions: one is about volume per store, the other about assortment within it. A single calculation separates them.

All fourteen stores with shortages run out of all four items at once, and the spread between items is almost zero. If assortment were the issue, one or two items would suffer, not the whole shelf. So the assortment branch is closed, and what remains is volume per store.
cards.note: Neighboring branches differ in what you would have to do: change the per-store delivery quota, or change the assortment within a store. Until you have calculated which one holds, there is nothing to base a decision on.

checks.q: Why is the “the data is wrong” branch checked before the others?
options: Otherwise conclusions on the other branches are worthless
It is the quickest one and needs no calculations at all
That is the custom in any analysis; it is a general rule
You'll be asked about it in the meeting, so check it early
checks.why: A duplicated week or mixed-up units produce a convincing and wrong answer, and the error will not show. The other three branches are calculated on the same data, so their results only make sense after the clean-up.

lessons.title: Hypothesis before data
lessons.summary: First a hypothesis and a way to disprove it, then the extract

cards.text:
The temptation to open the file and “see what's in there” is expensive: the extract has twenty thousand rows, and every one of them says something. Two hours later you will know a lot of interesting things, and none of them will be an answer.

So you write down a hypothesis first and only then go to the data. Not to confirm it, but to try to break it.

cards.heading: The hypothesis and what would kill it
cards.text: At Delta, the hypothesis was: there is enough volume, it is just in the wrong place. What would disprove it was stated up front as well.
list: If no store has a surplus, there is nowhere to take volume from, and the hypothesis is dead.
If write-offs and shortages occur at the same stores, distribution is not the problem.
If stores with shortages run out at random rather than towards the end of the week, the cause is something else.

cards.text:
The data did not break the hypothesis. Surpluses were found at 46 stores and shortages at 14, and they are different stores: the overlap is empty. Every single write-off is at a store with a surplus.

Note what exactly makes this result strong. Not that it matched expectations, but that before the calculation it was stated which outcome would force you to discard them.
cards.note: Write the line “I will drop this idea if…” before you calculate. Once you have seen the numbers, you can no longer write it honestly: for any result you will find a reason why it still confirms what you thought all along.

checks.q: A colleague says: “I'll look at the data and figure out what's going on.” What is wrong with that?
options: The data should only be reviewed together with the client
He has not said in advance what outcome would change his mind
The format of the future report needs to be agreed first
The extract is too large to be reviewed by eye
checks.why: Twenty thousand rows will contain support for almost any idea. Only one thing protects against that: stating, before the calculation, which result would force you to discard the hypothesis.

lessons.title: What the data does not contain
lessons.summary: Sales are not demand, and here that difference decides everything

cast.say: My shelves are empty by Thursday, and in your reports I'm a weak store.

cards.text:
There is no “demand” column in the extract, and there cannot be: the company only sees what it sold. If the product ran out on Friday, sales for the week equal what was delivered, not how many people wanted to buy.

The observation is capped from above, and it is not the customer who capped it but the company's own warehouse. In the file, such a store is indistinguishable from one where the product simply does not sell, and it looks weak precisely when it is the most starved of stock.

cards.heading: How to see it in the data
cards.text:
The signal is simple: in a row, sales are zero and stock is zero. So there was nothing to sell that day.

Before building conclusions on this, make sure the signal does not fire falsely. At Delta, the check took three queries.
list: Not a single row where sales are zero but stock is not: here, zero sales always means an empty shelf, never a lack of customers.
Out-of-stock days come in runs of two or three; the file has 672 such cases.
Out-of-stock runs end on delivery day: the truck arrives on Tuesday and sales resume.

cards.text:
There is no demand figure, so you need a proxy: the average daily sales rate on days when the product was in stock, multiplied by the number of days it was not. That gives 163,551 bottles over the quarter, 10.2% of all sales.

But the estimate rests on assumptions, and you are the one who must name them, not whoever catches you out in the meeting. Demand within the week is assumed to be flat, although Friday is higher than Monday. Promotion days are excluded from the rate calculation. A customer who did not find the product is assumed not to have come back later.

So the conclusion reads “we are losing at least 10% of sales under these assumptions”, not “exactly this much”.
cards.note: Write “at least”, not an exact number. Out-of-stock days tell you a sale could not happen, but not how many people walked away empty-handed. The loss cannot be smaller than calculated; it can easily be larger.

cast.say: A store's quota is based on its own sales. That's how we've always done it.

cards.heading: Why it does not correct itself
cards.text:
The delivered-to-sold ratio at stores with shortages is exactly one: they receive as much as they sold last time. At stores with a surplus it is around 1.3.

Then a loop kicks in. The store received too little, so it sold little; based on those sales, it was given the same quota for the following week; it received too little again. This repeats every week. From the outside it looks like a weak store, but the store is not to blame: its delivery quota has simply never been revisited.

So the report's conclusion is not “these stores are bad” but “the delivery quota is calculated from sales, when it should be calculated from demand”.

checks.q: A store sold little and spent all of Friday with zero stock. What does this mean?
options: Demand at the store is low; its volume should be cut
The store's data is wrong; it is better excluded
Sales hit the ceiling of what was delivered; demand is higher
The store was closed on Friday; it is an empty day
checks.why: Zero stock means there was nothing to sell: sales equal what was delivered, not demand. Cutting this store's volume deepens the shortage exactly where it already exists; a closed day would look different, with no numbers at all.

checks.q: Why is the conclusion phrased as “at least” rather than as an exact number?
options: To leave yourself a margin in case of a calculation error
That is the customary way to write reports for management
Nobody is going to check the exact figure anyway
Some observations are capped, so the estimate is a lower bound
checks.why: Out-of-stock days do not show how many people walked away empty-handed; that can only be estimated. An estimate based on the average rate understates the result, because shortages fall at the end of the week, when demand is above average.

units.title: From question to report
units.subtitle: The prompt for the model, the check, the upload and a name people can find it by

lessons.title: One report, one answer
lessons.summary: The most important rule: a report answers one question

cards.text:
Delta delivers packaged drinks to 60 stores in three cities. The warehouse ships once a week, on Tuesdays. The quarter has closed, and Delta's Head of Sales calls in the analyst, who is in their first month at the company.

The conversation opens with “why is everything going wrong”. You cannot write a report against that question: it is unclear what counts as the problem, rising write-offs, empty shelves or purchase volume. Until the question has been narrowed down to a single one, any report will be long and answer nothing.

So the first move is not to open the extract but to finish the sentence: “the report is needed to decide…”. If you cannot finish it, it is too early to start.

cast.say: Write-offs are up by a third, and empty-shelf complaints have doubled.

cards.text:
The analyst turns this into one question: which stores should get more product and which less, without buying more. That can be solved, and a report like this drives a decision: which store's quota to raise and which to lower.

The report's headline number is lost sales by store: how much a store would have sold had the product not run out before the next delivery. Not revenue. Revenue rises and falls for a dozen reasons at once, while lost sales tell you directly where to send the product.

The headline number goes at the top, in large type. Next to it, what we compare it with: the same store's actual sales. Detail on the other stores follows further down the page, for those who want it.
cards.note: Thirty metrics on a screen mean that none of them matters.

cards.heading: How to tell it worked
cards.text: Show the draft to someone who knows the business, and explain nothing out loud. The area manager visits the stores every week and will spot a gap faster than anyone. If they stumble on even one point, do not fix the labels or the colors; fix the question the report answers.
list: Your colleague can say within five seconds which number matters most here.
Your colleague understands, without your comments, whether that number is good or bad.
Your colleague does not ask “why is this here?”

cast.say: I can see the number. I can't see what I'm supposed to do with it.

checks.q: Your manager asks for a report title that is clear at a glance. Which title is best?
options: Lost sales by store · weekly
Quarterly sales extract report
Sales analytics, version two
Weekly summary of all stores
checks.why: A title names the decision, not the data source. “Lost sales by store · weekly” tells you why to open it; the other three tell you where the file came from, which does not help the reader.

lessons.title: The prompt for the model
lessons.summary: A ready-made prompt that produces a working file the first time

cards.text:
The analyst has an extract: 60 stores, 12 weeks, daily sales, deliveries, write-offs and stock for every item. Next to the date there is already the weekday and the week number, so that “deliveries on Tuesdays” can be seen rather than worked out. You can open it, but it is not obvious what to do with it.

The extract is the workbook delta-sales.xlsx with two sheets. Not everyone has Excel, so the same two sheets are also provided as plain files: delta-sales.csv for sales and delta-stock.csv for the warehouse. They open in Notepad and in any spreadsheet editor.

The report will be written by a model. Any model that can write code will do: what matters is not the name but how precise the prompt is.

The prompt has four parts: where the file will live, what it must look like, what question it answers and what your data looks like. The first two are the same for everyone and come ready-made. Only the third and fourth are yours: the decision the whole exercise is for, and the header row of your table.

cast.say: I have the extract. I don't have a report.

cards.note:
If you have no subscription of your own: duck.ai (Claude and GPT) and HuggingChat work without registration. With free registration: DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini.

Before your first prompt, ask IT which services the company allows: that is a decision for the security team, not for this course. The choice of service does not affect the data rule: only column headers and made-up rows ever leave your machine.

cards.heading: What is inside the file
cards.text:
Not everyone has Excel, and you may simply have nothing to open the workbook with. So here is everything it contains; reading it here is as good as reading the file itself.

The workbook has two sheets. The Sales sheet has 21,840 rows, one per store, item and day from 3 March to 25 May 2026. Below are the columns of this sheet with a sample value from the first row.

head: column
what it holds
example
rows: the day the row refers to
the same day as a word
week number from the start of the extract, 1 to 12
one of three: Riverton, Northfield, Lakeside
type of store: supermarket, convenience store, petrol station
what is sold: water 0.5, water 1.5, lemonade 0.5, iced tea 0.5
delivered that day, in units; zero on days with no delivery
written off that day, in units
how much is held at the store at the end of the day, in units

cards.note: The sales columns are in units, but two of the three cities keep their records in packs of 12 bottles. The extract itself says nothing about this: you find out by reconciling against the Warehouse sheet, where everything is always in bottles.

cards.heading: The second sheet: Warehouse
cards.text: 2,880 rows: what the warehouse shipped to each store on delivery day, and at what price. It is needed for reconciliation: without it there is no way to know how many bottles stand behind the word “pack”.

head: column
what it holds
example
rows: week number, same as on the Sales sheet
the delivery day, always a Tuesday
code of the store delivered to
how many bottles went to the store, always in bottles
price of one bottle; the currency is not stated in the file

cards.note: Both sheets are provided next to the workbook as plain files: delta-sales.csv for sales and delta-stock.csv for the warehouse. If you have no Excel, use those: a csv holds one table per file, so there are two files rather than one file with tabs.

cards.heading: The ready-made prompt
cards.text:
Copy it in full and replace the two lines in square brackets: the task and the data. Nothing else needs changing: the first two blocks are the same for any report on this platform.

The pair of lines “<data>” and “</data>” is a boundary. Everything between them the model reads as data, not as one more instruction; without the boundary, a header row is sometimes taken as a rule. The name inside the angle brackets does not matter; what matters is that the opening and closing lines match.

In the task line, the analyst writes their own question about lost sales by store. Inside the boundary go the column headers from your file and a couple of rows with made-up numbers.
cards.code_text:
Write a single HTML file: a report. I will open it with a double click,
check it and upload it to our internal platform, OnePage: there the report
is shown inside a page, in a sandboxed frame, with no internet access.

THE REPORT RECEIVES ITS DATA AS A FILE; NO DATA INSIDE IT
· On load, tell the platform you are ready to receive a file:
    window.parent.postMessage({type:'op_ready', slots:[0]}, '*')
· Receive it and parse it (e.data.data is an ArrayBuffer):
    window.addEventListener('message', function (e) {
      if (e.data && e.data.type === 'op_file' && e.data.slot === 0) { … }
    })
· If no file arrives within two seconds, show a “drop a file here” zone,
  so the report also works before it is uploaded to the platform.
· Accept .xlsx and .csv; detect the delimiter yourself (; or ,).
  Parse Excel with the SheetJS library; it is already on our server,
  at the same address as the report, and never goes outside:
      <script src="/static/js/vendor/xlsx.full.min.js"></script>
      var wb = XLSX.read(new Uint8Array(e.data.data), {type:'array'})
  When the file is opened with a double click from the desktop, that
  address does not exist: if XLSX did not load, say so on the page and
  accept .csv.
· Do not ask me to re-save the workbook as CSV, and do not write on the
  page that .xlsx cannot be read in the sandbox: on the platform it can.
· Normalize numbers: remove thousands separators (spaces), treat a comma
  as a decimal point. Read dates as both DD.MM.YYYY and YYYY-MM-DD.
· Embed the parsing code inside the file.

IMPORTANT
· Everything inside one file: no external links, no external fonts
  or libraries. The only exception is SheetJS at the address above: that
  is our server, not the internet.
· Do not use localStorage, cookies or IndexedDB; the sandbox has none.
· The report file itself must be under 1.5 MB (otherwise the list shows
  a placeholder instead of a live preview). This does not limit the size
  of the DATA file.
· Define colors as variables in :root and redraw charts on the event
  window.addEventListener('op:theme', redraw); the platform has light
  and dark themes.
· Headline number and comparison at the top, details below.

SO THAT I CAN CHECK IT
· At the bottom of the page, state how many rows were read and how many
  of them could not be parsed.
· Skip any row you could not parse and count it in that number.
· If something is missing from the data, say so on the page.
· Do not invent conclusions: write only what is calculated from the file.

TASK
[what the report must show and what decision is made based on it]

WHAT COLUMNS TO EXPECT
<data>
[paste the HEADER ROW of your file here (the column names) and add two
 or three rows with made-up numbers below it: the model needs the shape
 of the data, not the data itself]
</data>
cards.note: A rule with no exceptions: real data is never sent to external models (Claude, ChatGPT or any other), not a single row and not as a file. Not sales, not stock, not store names, not people's names. An external model needs the structure: what the columns are called and how the values are written. So the prompt gets your headers with made-up numbers underneath, and you open your own data in the finished report, where it stays with you.

cards.heading: Where the report gets your numbers from
cards.text:
The most common question from newcomers: if real data must not be shown to the model, where will it come from in the report?

The answer is in the first block of the prompt. The file the model writes is empty: it holds the calculation and the layout, but not a single figure of yours. It receives the numbers separately.
list: The model sees only the table header and made-up rows; that is enough to write the analysis.
You upload your real extract to the platform next to the report, in the “Slot 0 — initial data file” field.
The platform passes the file to the report whenever it is opened, and the report draws your numbers.
Before upload the report works the same way: it shows a “drop a file” zone, and you can test it on your laptop.
cards.note: So real data and the model never meet: the model worked with the structure, and the numbers appeared only on your side.

cards.heading: What each line of the prompt does
cards.text: None of the points is a matter of taste: each one prevents a specific failure.
list: “I will upload it to an internal platform, in a frame, with no internet”: a model writes the file differently when it knows where it will live: no external fonts, no outside requests, no reliance on browser storage.
“Everything inside one file”: a report with an external link shows a blank screen on the corporate network; this is the most common newcomer problem.
“Under 1.5 MB”: for heavier files the platform shows a placeholder in the list instead of a live preview.
“Headline number at the top”: people look at a report for a few seconds, and if the top is not the main point, they will not understand what it is about.

cards.heading: How to tell what broke
cards.text:
The “so that I can check it” block exists for exactly this. The finished report states at the bottom how many rows it read and how many it could not parse, and that one line answers the main debugging question: is it the data or the calculation?

If the bottom reads “read 21,840, not parsed 412”, it is the data: most likely the columns in those rows have shifted or the date is written differently. If nothing failed to parse but the number at the top still looks odd, it is the calculation, and you need to discuss it with the model.
list: The report must not fail entirely because of one bad row: skip it, count it, show the number.
Whatever was missing, the report states on the page rather than silently filling in.
Ask for one change at a time: otherwise it is unclear what actually helped.
cards.note: A report that silently skipped four hundred rows is more dangerous than one that did not open: you will fix the second today, and present the first to management.

cards.heading: Show the data, do not describe it
cards.text:
Write the task line the way you would explain it to a colleague from the next department: what must be visible and what decision is made based on it.

The data, however, should not be described in words; that is the most common mistake. The analyst does not retell the extract in words. They copy the header from the file (the row with the column names) and add two rows of made-up numbers below it. A sample like that shows at once which columns exist, how dates are written and what separates one value from the next.
cards.note: Any detail you leave out will be silently made up, and you will only find out from an odd number in the finished report.

cards.heading: Ready-made task block for Delta
cards.code_title: Put this into the TASK block
cards.text:
The TASK block in the prompt is the only place where you say WHAT to calculate. Whatever you write there is what the report will calculate; the other blocks are only about how it works technically.

For our case, the task reads as follows. Note that it says nothing about how to fix the data: you do not yet know what is peculiar about it yourself, and that is the right order. The first version of the report will be inaccurate, and the course will come back to that.
cards.code_text:
TASK
The report answers one question: how to reallocate the weekly delivery
volume between stores.

At the top, four numbers:
· how many bottles were lost over the period. Calculate it like this:
  take the days when sales are zero and stock is zero, and multiply them
  by that store's usual daily rate for that item;
· what share of actual sales this represents;
· how many stores had such days;
· which store lost the most.

Below, a table of ALL stores that had such days (there are usually
few), sorted by lost sales, descending. Columns: lost sales,
sold, and SALES RANK (the store's position in the list sorted
by sales). Do not truncate the table: it is the bottom rows that
decide the case. Sales rank is mandatory; without it the table
is meaningless.

Under the table, calculate in one line: how many of these stores
are among the 20 worst by sales.

Further down, in one sentence: how the usual rate was calculated and
why this is a lower bound rather than the exact size of the loss.
cards.note: “Sales rank” looks like a detail, but it is actually the key column of the report: it is what shows that stores with shortages look weak. The line under the table is its conclusion in a single number. Without these two things the report will push towards exactly the wrong decision.

cards.heading: Ready-made data block for Delta
cards.text:
So you do not have to build it yourself the first time, here is the same block, already filled in from the delta-sales.xlsx file from the first lesson. Press Copy and paste it into the prompt in place of the line in square brackets, together with the “<data>” and “</data>” lines.

In your own report you will do exactly the same: open your file, copy the row with the column names, add two rows of made-up numbers below it, and explain in words only those columns whose names are not obvious to everyone.

Sheet Sales, one row = store + item + day:
date;weekday;week;city;channel;store;item;sales;delivery;write-off;stock

04.03.2026;Wednesday;1;City-A;supermarket;ST-01;drink 0.5;193;0;0;1235

Sheet Warehouse, one row = what was delivered to a store on delivery day:
week;delivery date;store;item;shipped, btl;price per bottle
1;03.03.2026;ST-01;drink 0.5;1606;120
1;03.03.2026;ST-01;drink 1.5;1039;210

What the columns mean, where the name does not make it clear:
· sales, delivery, write-off, stock: units for that day;
· delivery is non-zero only on delivery day, which falls on a Tuesday;
· stock: how much is held at the store at the end of the day;
· “shipped, btl” on the Warehouse sheet is always in bottles, even where
  a store records its sales in packs.
</data>
cards.note: Not only the numbers are made up here, but the names too: the city, store and item have been replaced with dissimilar ones. The model needs the SHAPE of a record (how many columns, in what order, what a date and the decimal separator look like), not your real values. None of this will end up in the file it writes: the report reads the names from the extract itself.

cards.heading: If the answer is not right
cards.text: The first version is rarely the last, and that is no reason to fix the file by hand. Ask for corrections in the same words you would use with a colleague. One request, one change: that way you can see exactly what changed it, and it is easy to step back.
list: “Too much going on: keep one headline number and the comparison.”
“Don't touch the data, change only the layout.”
“Make it readable on a laptop, not just on a large screen.”

cards.heading: How to get a file out of the answer
cards.text:
The model returns its result in one of two ways. Either with a download button, in which case the file is ready. Or as text right in the conversation, and that is what confuses people most often: it seems something is missing, although the report is right in front of you.

In the second case, copy the entire answer, paste it into a text editor (Notepad on Windows, TextEdit in plain-text mode on a Mac) and save it under any name ending in .html. The extension matters more than the name: without it the file opens as text, not as a report.
list: Save it with the .html extension, not .txt and not .docx.
The file name does not matter on the platform: the report will have its own title there.
Once saved, open it with a double click: the report should open in the browser as a normal page.
cards.note: While the file sits on your laptop it is a draft that only you can see. The course has two more steps: check it in a minute and upload it to the platform; until it is uploaded, the report does not exist for the company. If things did not work out with the model, the upload lesson contains a finished report built on this same extract: you can practice with it and come back to the prompt later.

checks.q: The model suggests: “let's load the charting library via a link; that makes the file lighter.” How do you respond?
options: Agree: that really does make the file lighter
Ask for all the code to be embedded in the file
Agree, and send the library separately later
Drop the charts from the report altogether
checks.why: On the platform the report opens in a closed frame with no internet access. Anything loaded via a link simply will not load, and instead of a chart there will be a blank screen.

lessons.title: Check before you upload
lessons.summary: Nice-looking numbers prove nothing: reconcile them with the source

cards.text:
The file is saved, a double click, and the report opens. The numbers are there, the charts are drawn, and one week in May comes out as a record: exactly twice the usual sales. The manager is pleased.

The analyst checks it against the deliveries sheet: there is just one shipment that week, yet sales doubled. The reason is simple: the week was exported twice and sits in the file twice.

The item shares did not give the fake away: everything doubled at once, and the ratio between items stayed the same to three decimal places. The model did not lie. It calculated exactly what it was given.

cast.say: A record week! What did we do right?

cards.heading: What to look at
cards.text: Nice-looking numbers prove nothing: a record nobody can explain is a reason to check, not to celebrate. What catches it is not looking at the report but reconciling with the source, and that takes a minute: before upload, not after the first question at the team meeting.
list: Did it open at all, and did everything render?
Do the numbers look like the ones in your table? A model can round silently.
Is it readable on a laptop, not just on a large monitor?
Can you see within three seconds which number matters most?

cards.text:
The second finding that same evening: one store was closed for refurbishment for five days. The rows for those days in the extract are blank, not zero, and those are different things. Blank means the store was not trading. Zero means the store was trading but had no product.

If you treat blank as zero, that store's average daily sales drop by 6%, and the refurbishment week looks like a sales collapse that never happened.

If something does not add up, do not fix it yourself. Tell the model which number is wrong and what it should be, and ask it to redo the report. This is a normal way of working, not a defeat.
cards.note: Checking takes a minute. The “our numbers here are wrong” conversation takes weeks.

cast.say: There was scaffolding up for five days. There were no sales, and there couldn't have been.

checks.q: One week in the report came out at exactly twice the usual level. What do you do first?
options: Show it to the manager: finally some good news
Reconcile that week with the warehouse deliveries sheet
Ask the model to generate the report one more time
Remove that week so it does not distort the picture
checks.why: A record nobody can explain is most often duplicated rows, not a good week. Item shares do not change when everything doubles, so they will not tell you anything; only reconciling with the source will, and it takes a minute.

lessons.title: Upload to the platform
lessons.summary: Five steps from a file on your laptop to an address you can share

cards.text:
The report is ready and sits on the analyst's laptop. The manager travels between cities and opens everything on a phone, so emailing the file is pointless: a week later they will be holding an old version, and neither of you will know.

Once uploaded, the report gets its own address on the platform. The link can be shared, opened on a phone or shown in a meeting, and everyone sees the same thing, because there is one file, not a copy for each person.

cards.heading: Step 1. Open the upload page
cards.text: In the left-hand menu, choose “Upload”. The buttons below are named exactly as they appear on screen.

cards.heading: Step 2. Drop in the file
cards.text:
Drag the file into the frame, or click it and pick the file on your disk. .html and .htm are accepted.

The “Detect type” and “Configure slots” steps in the bar at the top are handled by the platform: it looks at what is inside the file, and for a self-contained report there is nothing to do there.

cards.heading: If you don't have your own report yet
cards.text:
You can practice even without a successful answer from the model. Both files are here: a Delta report, already written and built the right way (no data inside; it receives it), and the same sales extract.

Download both, open the report with a double click and drag the extract into it: you will see the finished analysis. This is exactly what you should end up with using your own data.
cards.note: Then upload both to the platform: the report as usual, and the extract into the data field that appears in the next step.

cards.heading: Step 3. Attach the data
cards.text:
The platform recognizes a report that reads a file and shows a data field labeled “Slot 0 — initial data file”. Choose your extract there: .xlsx, .xls, .csv and a few other formats are accepted.

From then on, the platform hands this file to the report every time it is opened. When fresh data arrives, you replace the file; the report itself does not need rewriting.
cards.note: No field visible? Then the report does not ask for a file: the data is inside it. That works too, but updating such a report will have to go through the model.

cards.heading: Step 4. Title and publishing
cards.text:
“Title” is the only required field: it is how people will find the report in the list. “Description” is one line about the decision the report supports.

The “Publish immediately” box is ticked by default, meaning the report becomes available to colleagues right away. Untick it if you want to review it yourself first.
cards.note: There is no folder on this page: the report goes into the shared list, and you can sort it into folders later, right there.

cards.heading: Step 5. Publish
cards.text: The “Publish dashboard” button at the bottom of the card. After that the report opens at its own address, and that is the link you send to colleagues.

cards.heading: What you end up with

cast.say: Opened it in the car on the way to the warehouse. It works.

cards.text:
The report lives on the platform: it has an address, it can be viewed on a phone, and everyone is looking at the same file.

It worked if the report opened and looks the same as it did on your laptop. If the file was not accepted, the cause is almost always the file itself, not permissions: open it with a double click again and check that everything is in place.
cards.note: You can re-upload the file as many times as you like; it will not create a second report.

checks.q: The report is uploaded and opens for you, but your manager writes “no access”. What do you check first?
options: The file size: perhaps it is far too heavy
Their browser: maybe another one is needed
The report title: perhaps they searched for the wrong one
Whether the report is published and they have access
checks.why: A draft is visible only to you. Publishing and the access list are two separate settings, both on the report's page.

task.text: Upload your Delta report. If your prompt to the model has not produced a working file yet, take the ready-made sample and the extract from the “If you don't have your own report yet” card.
task.hint: I can't see any report that you own yet. Upload a file on the Upload page and come back.

lessons.title: A name people can find
lessons.summary: The title is what people will find you by a month from now

cards.text:
A month goes by. On the platform the analyst has “report”, “report_final”, “report_final_2”, “final_fixed” and one more whose name they no longer remember. The manager asks for the one about empty shelves.

Opening all five in turn is the price of a bad name. And it has to be paid every single time. A year from now the shared list will hold two hundred reports, and the one that gets found is the one with a clear title.

cast.say: Send me the one about empty shelves.

cards.heading: The three-part rule
cards.text: A title is built from three parts, and that is almost always enough. Any order, any separator: what matters is not the look but that each part answers its own question. Check your last report: does it have all three?
list: What it is about: “Lost sales”, “Write-offs”, “Stock”.
Who or what it covers: a store, a city, the whole network.
What period: a week, a month, a quarter.

cards.text:
“Lost sales · stores · week” is found in a second. Nobody will ever find “report_final_v2_fixed”, you included.

A common mistake is putting a date or a version number in the title. The report lives on: its data will be refreshed, while “May” in the name stays and confuses everyone.

The test is simple: imagine you are looking for this report six months from now and remember only its topic. You can rename it at any time; the address does not change.
cards.note: The description is one line about the decision this report supports. That is enough.

checks.q: Which title for a store report will still work six months from now?
options: Report for the manager, as asked
Final summary 05.2026 (fixed)
Dashboard No. 4: stores, deliveries
Lost sales · stores · week
checks.why: A title should say what the report is about, what it covers and for what period. A number, a date and the word “final” mean nothing six months later, whereas “Lost sales · stores · week” can be found with a single word.

task.text: Star a report you will keep coming back to. Favorites rise to the top of the list.
task.hint: No favorites yet. Click the star next to any row in the report list.

units.title: Access, updates, presenting
units.subtitle: Who can see it, how to update the data and what to do when something breaks

lessons.title: Who will see the report
lessons.summary: Who to show the report to, and who to trust with updating it

cards.text:
The manager asks you to show the report to the financial controller, who is costing the shortages and wants to look at the numbers himself. He is not on the platform: he never logs in and will not set up an account for a single report.

You could email the file, but a week later he will be holding an old version, and you will have no way of noticing.

Every report has its own access list, and by default only you can see it. This is not the platform being fussy: people build first and decide who to show it to afterwards.

cast.say: Show it to Finance. They're not on the platform.

cards.heading: Four options: three for viewing, one for updating
cards.text:
The first three are about reading. Which one to choose depends not on how important the report is, but on who will read it: a colleague with an account, the whole platform, or someone with no account, like that financial controller. Getting it wrong is no disaster: you can change the option at any time.

The fourth stands apart: it is about who is allowed to change the data in the report.
list: Name colleagues individually: the most common case.
Open it to everyone who signs in to the platform: for shared reports.
Create a link: for people without an account on the platform.
Grant the right to update data: to whoever will load fresh extracts instead of you.

cast.say: The extract reaches me on Tuesday morning. I can upload it myself.

cards.heading: The right to update data
cards.text:
A report lives for weeks, and you go on holiday. To keep it from going stale, the right to load new data is given to whoever receives that data first, and most often that is not the analyst.

This right opens everything except deletion: the person can upload a new version, edit the description and set up access, but cannot delete the report. There is no need to hand over ownership for this, and you should not: there is one owner, and the owner is accountable for the report.
cards.note: Viewing and updating are different things. A link and “open to everyone” only allow viewing; you cannot load new data through them.

cards.text:
“Open to everyone” means all employees on the platform, not the whole internet. A link requires no sign-in (it opens without an account), but it only opens from inside the corporate network: the platform itself is not reachable from outside.

So you cannot show a report via a live link to someone outside the company, and that is not a limitation of the report but how access works. If you need to share outside, export the numbers and send them separately, following your security team's rules.

A more common problem is closer to home: sending the report's address and forgetting to add the person to the access list. They see a “no access” page and conclude the report is broken; you find out a week later. Access first, then the address.
cards.heading: Where “sharing” ends
cards.note: A link that went to the wrong place can be closed: access through it stops working immediately. The easiest way to check that everything is visible is to ask a colleague to open the link while you watch.

checks.q: The supply planning manager will update the data in your report every week. What should you give him?
options: Make him the report owner in your place
Grant him the right to update the report's data
Send him a link to the report with no sign-in
Open the report to every employee in the company
checks.why: The right to update data opens everything except deletion: he can upload new versions but cannot delete the report. A link and “open to everyone” only allow viewing.

task.text: Create a link to any of your reports: open it, go to the Share tab on the right and click Generate. You can close the link at any time.
task.hint: I can't see any link you have created yet. Open your report, go to the Share tab on the right, click Generate and come back.

lessons.title: Update the data
lessons.summary: A new file in the report, not a new report next to it

cast.say: It's Tuesday and I have the extract. Where do I put it?

cards.text:
A new week has arrived, and with it a new extract. The temptation is simple: create a second report and publish it alongside the first.

Here is what happens next. Half the department spends the week looking at the old report: some have it bookmarked, some have it in a chat, and their favorite star is on it too. Decisions are made on last week's numbers, and nobody understands what is wrong.

cards.heading: Data changes inside the report itself
cards.text:
Open the report and expand the panel on the right. The Data tab holds the file the report reads.

Choose the new file in the “Data slots” section and click “Upload slots”. That's it: a second later the report shows fresh numbers.
cards.note: The report itself does not change by a single byte; only the file it reads changes.

cards.heading: What stays in place
cards.text: This is exactly why you replace the file rather than publish a new report: the address, the access list and your colleagues' habits are worth more than one week's figures.
list: The report's address: old links keep working.
The access list: nobody needs to be added again.
Its place in the shared list, and the favorite star your colleagues gave it.
The report's version number: it is about the report, not the data.

cards.heading: If the report itself has changed
cards.text:
Data and the report itself are updated in different places, and the difference is worth keeping in mind. A new calculation, a different chart, a fixed bug: that is a new version of the report. Versions tab, “New version” section, “Upload new version” button. The version number goes up; the address and access stay the same.

Previous versions do not disappear: they are listed right there, each with a “Restore” button. So updating is not risky: if the new version turns out to have a bug, going back is a single click.
cards.note: A restore moves forward, not backward: the contents of the old version are laid down as a new version on top of the current one. No history is lost: the restore itself appears in the list and can be rolled back too. The data stays current: what comes back is the report's calculation and look, not that week's figures.

cards.text: If data arrives regularly, set yourself a fixed day. At Delta it is Tuesday, delivery day: the extract in the morning, the new file in the report by lunchtime. Then colleagues stop asking how fresh the numbers are and start coming to the report on their own.
cards.note: A new report alongside = a new link = half the people looking at old numbers.

checks.q: A fresh extract has arrived; the report's calculation has not changed. What do you do?
options: Upload a new version of the report in the Versions tab
Publish a second report next to it, marked “new”
Replace the file in the Data tab with “Upload slots”
Ask colleagues to reopen the report and refresh the page
checks.why: The report did not change; the data did, and it lives in a separate file. A report version is needed when the calculation or the layout changes; a new report alongside simply leaves half the department on the old link.

lessons.title: Present it in a meeting
lessons.summary: A live report on screen: on its own or as a slide in a presentation

cards.text:
The weekly team meeting. On the slide is a screenshot of the report taken the evening before. The analyst states the headline number: this is how much the stores missed out on in sales over the quarter. The supply planning manager asks bluntly: why should we believe this?

It is a fair question. There is no demand in the extract, only sales, and they stop where the product ran out. Lost sales were calculated with a proxy: the average daily sales rate before the product ran out, multiplied by the number of out-of-stock days.

cast.say: Why should we believe this?

cards.heading: The answer rests on assumptions
cards.text: So the conclusion is not “we are losing exactly this much” but “we are losing at least this much, under three assumptions, and here they are”. An assumption stated out loud does not weaken the report; it ends the argument: from then on people discuss a specific condition, not your integrity.
list: Demand within the week is assumed flat; in reality the end of the week is higher.
The promotion week is excluded from the rate calculation; otherwise the rate is inflated.
A customer who did not find the product did not come back for it; some did, so this estimate is high.

cards.text:
You cannot show assumptions on a picture or open up the detail, and the picture itself went stale the evening it was taken. Promising “I'll send it after the meeting” means losing both the decision and a week.

So what you show is not a snapshot but the report itself. The platform offers two ways to do this, and the choice between them is the choice between “one report” and “several slides in a row”.

cards.heading: One report: the Present button
cards.text:
Open the report and click “Present” in the top right. The three options do different things:

“Fullscreen”: the report fills the screen with no menus or panels, which is what you want on a projector. “In this tab”: the same, but within the browser window. “New tab”: a separate tab, so you can open it in advance and not hunt for it in front of everyone.

Press Esc to exit. The report stays live throughout: you can hover over it, expand a detail and answer a question right there on the screen.

cards.heading: Several slides: Presentations
cards.text:
When the story is longer than one report, build a presentation: Presentations in the left-hand menu, the “+ create presentation” tile, then “Add slide”.

A slide can be a report (it opens live, not as a picture), a PNG or JPG image up to 5 MB, a PDF up to 20 MB (with a checkbox, it is split into one slide per page), or a ready-made HTML file up to 10 MB. You set the order by dragging, and every slide has a field for notes.

cards.heading: The day before: Verify before show
cards.text:
This button goes through every slide and shows, for each one, the report's publication date and the date of the data it was built from, flagging any that are out of date or no longer open. A minute the day before is worth it, so you are not hunting for a missing slide in front of everyone.

During the show, the ← → arrows move between slides, Space goes forward, F switches to full screen and Esc exits. The presentation is visible only to you: you show colleagues your screen, you do not give them access.
cards.note: The report does not go out to the internet; the corporate network is all it needs. So in the meeting room it opens just as it does at your desk.

checks.q: At the team meeting you are asked why the report's headline number can be trusted. Which response is strongest?
options: Say that the data came straight from the warehouse
Point to the model: it did the calculation
Promise to send a detailed calculation afterwards
Open the report and state the assumptions aloud
checks.why: There is no demand in the data; the number was calculated with a proxy, so trust rests on the assumptions, not the source. A live report on the slide lets you show them and the detail right away instead of promising to send them.

lessons.title: If something goes wrong
lessons.summary: Four common problems and what to do about them

cards.text:
The report opens for everyone except the supply planning manager, who gets a blank screen. Nothing is broken: the file still contains a link to a font on the internet, and the corporate network has no internet. At home, the analyst's copy fetched the font and opened; the manager's copy has nowhere to fetch it from.

Almost all report problems come down to four, and each is fixed in a minute if you know where to look. The first step is always the same: find out what the other person sees, not what you see.

cast.say: I get a blank screen. Does it open for you?

cards.heading: What happened
cards.text: The order is always the same: look at what the person sees, reproduce it yourself, and change one thing at a time.

head: Symptom
What to do
rows: The file links to something outside. Open the file in Notepad, search for “http” and ask the model to embed that inside the file
The report takes a long time to load

The data is baked into the file itself. Ask the model to rework the report so that it READS a data file (the prompt from the “The prompt for the model” lesson), and upload the extract to slot 0 on the Data tab
The browser is showing its own copy. Reload the page and clear the cache: Ctrl+Shift+R (Windows) or ⌘+Shift+R (Mac)
The report is not published or the person is not on the access list: Settings tab, “Published” checkbox; Access tab, add the person

cards.note: If Ctrl+Shift+R does not help, open the report in an incognito window (Ctrl+Shift+N in Chrome and Edge): there is no cache there at all, and you can tell at once whether it is the browser or the report itself.

cards.text:
Most often it turns out to be the first row: the file fetches something from the internet, and the corporate network has no internet, so outside it opened and inside it goes blank. The second most common is “I'm seeing old numbers”, and that is almost always the browser, not the platform.

If that does not help, write to platform support and attach the file itself. There is no shame in it; it is faster.
cards.note: Include three things in your message: what you clicked, what you expected to see and what you saw instead.

checks.q: A store report takes ten seconds to open. What is the most common cause?
options: Too much data inside the report file itself
The platform server is slow at that hour
A weak laptop or a congested network
The report is unpublished and so is slow
checks.why: The server sends the file in a fraction of a millisecond. The rest of the time the browser is parsing what is inside: the more data baked into the file, the longer it takes to open.

checks.q: The report opened at home, but on the platform it shows a blank white screen. Where do you start?
options: Upload the file again in case it was cut short
Ask the administrator for more permissions
Check whether the file has any external links
Make the file smaller and try once more
checks.why: A blank screen almost always means one thing: something is loaded via an internet link, and the report's frame cannot go there. Ask the model to embed it inside the file.

units.title: Working with the model
units.subtitle: What to delegate, how to explain the task and how to spot a mistake within a minute

lessons.title: What to delegate and what to decide yourself
lessons.summary: The model builds the file; you choose what it means

cards.text:
The manager suggests something simple: let the model decide which metric goes at the top. After all, it has seen thousands of reports.

It won't. The model is quick at the things that would take you an evening: calculating, building the file, laying out the numbers in sections, labeling charts and redoing all of it as many times as you ask. But it does not know why you came. What matters more, revenue by city or lost sales by store, depends on the decision that will be made, and a person makes that decision.

cast.say: Let the model decide what matters here.

cards.heading: Split it up in advance
cards.text: It helps to draw the line before you open the model's window. Then the conversation is short: you are not debating with it what counts as important, you are asking it to do what you have already decided.
list: Yours: the question the report answers, the headline number and a fair comparison for it.
The model's: the calculation, layout, styling, chart labels and any number of revisions.
Together: the presentation; you ask for two or three ways of showing the same thing and pick one.

cards.text:
A useful habit: before opening the model's window, finish that same sentence, “the report is needed to decide…”. Until it is finished, any prompt will be long and vague, and the answer will need reworking.

Once the sentence is ready, the brief takes one line: you name the decision, show the data and hand everything else to the model. It is not about trusting it; it is about who is accountable for the decision the report will drive.
cards.note: If you cannot explain the task to a colleague in a minute, you will not be able to explain it to a model either.

checks.q: You have not decided which number goes at the top. The model offers to choose for you. What is best?
options: Ask for three options and choose yourself
Agree: it has seen more reports than you
Put it off until someone more senior decides
Put every metric at the top all at once
checks.why: Choosing the headline number is choosing the decision the report drives, and you are accountable for it. Asking for options is useful: the model widens the list, but the final word stays with a person.

lessons.title: How to explain the task
lessons.summary: A data sample instead of a description in words

cards.text:
The analyst's first attempt went like this: “there's a date column, then city, then store, then sales, in bottles I think”. The model filled in the rest by itself and said nothing about it: the delimiter, the column order, the date format, the units.

Everything you leave unsaid will be silently made up, and that is the most common cause of odd numbers.

Instead of a description, give a sample: a few rows with headers, exactly as they look in your file. It is shorter than any explanation, can be checked in a second and leaves no room for guesswork.

cast.say: I explained it in words, and it made up the units.

cards.heading: Three labeled sections
cards.text:
A prompt is easiest to structure in three parts: data, task, constraints. This is what a prompt for the sales extract looks like, with made-up numbers instead of real ones. The column headers are yours; the numbers are invented. The model needs the structure. From two rows it can see the delimiter, the date format and that stock is a separate column, and it also infers the types: nobody declares them in an extract, and the only way to tell that “03.03.2026” is a date, “1 234,56” a number and “RV-01” text is from how the value is written. So write your made-up numbers in the same format as the real ones: a foreign date format in the sample means a foreign parser in the report. You change the task line to suit your question and leave the constraints as they are.

The “<data>…</data>” boundary separates the sample from the instructions: between those lines the model sees only data. This is Anthropic's own recommendation for prompts where instructions and data sit together, and other models understand it too.
cards.code_text:
DATA (first, before everything else)
<data>
date; weekday; week; city; store; item; sales; delivery; stock
12.05.2026; Tuesday; 11; city A; ST-07; item 1; 120; 480; 340
13.05.2026; Wednesday; 11; city A; ST-07; item 1; 0; 0; 0
</data>

TASK
One screen: how much in sales the stores lost because the product ran out before the next delivery.

CONSTRAINTS
· One file, everything inside, no external links.
· Same units as in the sample; do not convert anything.
· If data is missing, ask; do not fill in the gaps.

cards.text:
Three labeled sections work better than one paragraph: the model does not confuse the conditions with the data, and it is easier for you to fix a single line later. Put the sample first: what comes at the start of a prompt gets lost less often than what sits in the middle.

And a rule with no exceptions: real commercial and personal data is not sent to external models, the ones you open in a separate browser tab. Five made-up rows with your headers are enough for a sample: the structure matters, not the content.

Inside the platform it works differently. In the Explore section the calculation runs on the company's server, and the model receives only column names and types, not a single cell of data. So there you can ask about the real numbers.
cards.note: The line “if data is missing, ask” saves the most time: without it, whatever is missing will be silently made up.

checks.q: The model needs to understand how the store sales extract is structured. What do you give it?
options: A description in words of each column and its type
The header and two rows, written as in the file
The whole quarter's extract, so it makes no mistakes
The file name, the row count and a list of types
checks.why: Types are not declared anywhere in an extract: neither a csv nor an Excel workbook states them. The model infers them from HOW a value is written: 03.03.2026 is a date in day-first format, 1 234,56 is a number with a space as the thousands separator and a comma as the decimal mark, RV-01 is text rather than a number, and an empty cell is not zero. So the made-up rows are written in exactly the same format as the real ones: a list of types in words is shorter but does not say how to read them.

checks.q: What from a sales extract may you paste into a prompt to an external model?
options: Contact details of the store managers
The whole quarter's extract, for accuracy
Column headers and five made-up rows
Real sales for every store in the network
checks.why: Only the structure goes to an external model: what the columns are called and how the values are written. Real numbers, store names and certainly people's contact details stay in your file; you open the finished report on them on your own side.

lessons.title: Anonymize an extract in five minutes
lessons.summary: Anonymizer: a file with names and tax IDs becomes a safe sample

cards.text:
The previous step asks you to show the model a SAMPLE record: the header and a couple of rows. But in a real extract those rows contain people's names, tax IDs, phone numbers and customer names. Inventing replacements by hand takes a long time and is error-prone: forget one column and it leaks.

The platform has a dedicated page for this: Anonymizer. It replaces values while keeping the shape of the record: length, format, separators. Below are six steps, one screen each.
cards.note: The buttons below are named exactly as they appear on screen.

cards.heading: Practice on this file
cards.text: A training workbook: eight customers with names, tax IDs and phone numbers, a hidden sheet with a discount lookup table, a link to someone else's workbook and a colleague's comment. All of it is made up: it is a deliberately “bad file”, like most files in real life. Work through the steps on it.

cards.heading: Step 1. Open Anonymizer
cards.text: It is in the left-hand menu, between Explore and Quests.

cards.heading: Step 2. Drop in the file
cards.text: Drag the workbook into the frame, or click it and choose the file. .xlsx, .xls, .xlsb, .csv and .ods are accepted, up to 10 MB.
cards.note: The file is not sent anywhere: the page is locked down so that it physically cannot make a network request. Parsing and replacement happen in your browser; the workbook goes neither to us nor anywhere else.

cards.heading: Step 3. Read what else is in the workbook
cards.text: The first thing the page shows is a list of what would travel with the file besides the visible tables. These are not errors but a reminder: almost nobody remembers what is in their workbook.
list: hidden sheets, and “very hidden” ones that do not even appear in the sheet menu;
named ranges, which are usually a lookup table;
links to other files: the path alone reveals the project and the drive;
formulas, comments, and hidden rows and columns;
the author's name in the workbook properties.
cards.note: The page removes none of this: only you know what is superfluous here. Delete what you do not need in Excel and run the file through again.

cards.heading: Step 4. Check the columns
cards.text:
Next comes the column table: what was found, what it will be replaced with, and a “Mask” checkbox. Ticked are the columns that look like personal data (tax ID, phone, full name, email) and text where almost every value is unique. Numbers and dates are left alone; otherwise the file would no longer add up.

Tick by hand anything the tool treats as a harmless category but which, in your case, is customers: in the screenshot, exactly those columns were left unticked. The “Replace with” column says what to replace with: keep as is, full name, tax ID, city, code.
cards.note: Codes like ST-01 remain codes of the same shape, and the same value is replaced identically across the whole workbook; otherwise two sheets would no longer join.

cards.heading: Step 5. Press the button
cards.text: “Generate masked file”, and the browser saves a file next to the original with the same name and a __masked suffix. That is your safe copy.

cards.heading: Step 6. Take the sample and read the self-check
cards.text:
A summary appears below the table. It contains two things.

The first is a ready-made sample for the prompt: the header and three already anonymized rows, with a “Copy sample” button. That is what goes into the data block, not the whole file.

The second is the self-check: which columns still hold real values. If customers or store addresses are among them, go back to step 4, tick them and press the button again.

cards.heading: What anonymization does not do
cards.text: It does not make the file public. The numbers and dates are still real, and a rare combination of them can sometimes identify a person even without a name; the self-check warns about such columns separately.
list: what goes into the conversation with the model is a three-row SAMPLE, not the whole file;
an anonymized file is no reason to share it publicly;
if a rule depends on real values, it belongs in a setting inside the report, not in the prompt.
cards.note: The reverse is also true: an anonymized file remains usable. Links between sheets are preserved, numbers and dates are untouched, and it produces the same totals as the original.

takeaways: A sample for the model is made with a tool, not by hand: a forgotten column is a leak.
Anonymizer runs in the browser; the file goes nowhere, including to us.
Before sending, check what else is in the workbook: a hidden sheet or an external link travels with it.

checks.q: Anonymizer found a hidden sheet with a lookup table in the workbook. What will it do with it?
options: Remove it from the anonymized file
Nothing: it will only warn you about it
Replace the values on that sheet too
Refuse to process such a workbook
checks.why: Only the file's author knows which findings are superfluous: a hidden sheet may be junk or a lookup table that is needed. So the page names the findings, and the person removes them, in Excel, before the next run.

checks.q: You have anonymized an extract. What do you send to the model?
options: The whole anonymized file, since it is safe
The original file: the anonymized one adds up worse
Nothing: the model needs no data at all
The three sample rows from the summary panel
checks.why: The model needs the shape of a record, not the data: how many columns, in what order, what a date and the decimal separator look like. That is exactly the three rows from the summary panel. There is no reason to send the file itself, even anonymized.

lessons.title: Check the answer in a minute
lessons.summary: Three checks that catch almost any mistake

cards.text:
The supply planning manager brings his own shipments report: for two cities his volume is twelve times higher than in the analyst's report. Both files are tidy, and both are internally consistent.

The answer is not in the arithmetic: two of the three cities keep records in packs of 12 bottles, the third in bottles. The extract has one column with one name, but different counting rules. Nobody made a mistake.

The model said nothing, because a model makes mistakes in an even voice: a made-up number sounds just as calm as a correct one. So checking is not distrust; it is a normal part of the work.

cast.say: My shipments are twelve times higher. What units are you using?

cards.heading: Each check takes twenty seconds
cards.text: Three actions in a row, and none of them requires recalculating the whole report.
list: Check three numbers against the table: the total, the largest and the smallest. A mistake is usually visible straight away.
Ask to see the intermediate calculation: what was added, what was divided, which rows were dropped and why.
Ask the same question from the other side: after “where were the biggest losses”, ask where they were smallest. The answers should agree.

cards.text:
Found a discrepancy? Do not ask “are you sure?”: you will get polite agreement and learn nothing. Say which number is wrong and what it should be, and ask for the file to be rebuilt.

Two or three short rounds of “here it is, fix this” are more reliable than one very long prompt: in each round you see the result and fix one thing. And write the units right into the report: then the next argument about packs versus bottles ends before it starts.
cards.note: A matching total proves nothing yet: errors often cancel each other out. A total that does not match means there is definitely an error, and you need to find it.

checks.q: The store report is ready, and the numbers look plausible. What do you do first?
options: Ask the model whether it is sure of its calculation
Check the total and the two extreme values
Show the report to a colleague and wait for comments
Publish it and fix it if anyone notices
checks.why: Asking “are you sure?” checks nothing: the model confirms right and wrong with equal calm. Reconciling with the source takes half a minute and catches both silent rounding and lost rows.

checks.q: Why ask the model for the intermediate calculation?
options: To make the report look more detailed to the reader
To make the model work more slowly and carefully
To have an answer ready for any question asked
To see what was added up and what was dropped
checks.why: The mistake is almost never in the arithmetic but in which rows went into the calculation and which fell out. Seeing the intermediate steps, you find that spot in seconds instead of recalculating the whole report.

lessons.title: Your name is on the report
lessons.summary: A person, not the model, is accountable for the numbers

cards.text:
The weekly team meeting. The store report is on screen, and the manager asks about one of the top rows: where do the lost sales at this store come from, if it sells less than its neighbors?

The question is put to the analyst, not the model. “That's what the model calculated” is not an answer; it is the same as “that's what came out of the spreadsheet”: the tool is named, but there is no explanation. Answering that question is precisely the work the report was made for.

cast.say: I'm asking you, not the model.

cards.heading: Your figure differs from someone else's report
cards.text: The packs story will repeat itself many times, and it is always resolved the same way. Someone else's report is almost never wrong; it is about something else: a different period, a different set of stores or different units.
list: Do not argue about who is right: first find where the counting rules diverge.
Check three things: the period, the set of rows (who was included) and the units.
Add a line to the report stating what was counted and for what period.

cards.text:
It is worth saying plainly that the file was built with the help of a model, and adding that you checked the numbers against the source. This is not an admission of weakness: the reader needs to know that a check was done and whom to contact if they still find a mistake.

A report with nobody behind it gets skimmed; a report someone is accountable for gets opened every week. One line at the end heads off half of all future questions.

cast.say: The model built the file. I checked the numbers.

cards.heading: Where to learn more
cards.text: This unit adapts Anthropic's openly available materials to our task. The original sources are free.
list: AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations: a course on four skills: what to delegate, how to describe the task, how to evaluate the answer and what you are accountable for. anthropic.com/ai-fluency
Prompting best practices: a reference of prompting techniques: examples, sections, ordering of parts. platform.claude.com/docs
anthropics/courses on GitHub: the same techniques with exercises, if you want practice.

checks.q: Your report and the warehouse's report show different shipment volumes. Where do you start?
options: Write that they have an error and attach the file
Check the period, the set of rows and the units
Rebuild the report from scratch and compare
Ask the model which of the reports is correct
checks.why: Different numbers almost always mean different counting rules, not someone's mistake: a different period, a different set of rows or different units. Until the rules have been compared, arguing about who is right leads nowhere.

checks.q: A mistake has been found in a report the model built. Who is accountable?
options: The model: it did the calculation, not you
Nobody: it is a draft that everyone looks at
You: it is published under your name
The platform: it accepted a file with an error
checks.why: Here the model is a tool, just like a formula in a spreadsheet, and the report carries your name. So you are the one who acknowledges and fixes the mistake, and quickly: the longer a wrong number stays up, the more decisions get made on it.

units.title: See it through to an answer
units.subtitle: Check the data, fix the report, reconcile the numbers and turn them into a decision

lessons.title: Read your own report
lessons.summary: What the first version shows, and why it is too early to trust it

cards.text:
The report is published, the link has gone out, the manager has opened it and asked exactly the question everything started with.

The report does not answer it by itself. It shows numbers; the answer has to be read off them and put into words. This is the step people skip most often: the file is ready, so the job is done. The job is not done until there is one sentence you can say at the team meeting.

cast.say: I've seen the report. So what do I do with it?

cards.heading: Four numbers, all from your report
cards.text: Open your report and write down four numbers. Do not paraphrase; actually write them down: “there are a lot of losses” will not survive the first question, “how much?”.
list: how many bottles in sales were lost over 12 weeks: the big number at the top;
what share of actual sales that is: next to it, as a percentage;
at how many stores the product ran out before delivery;
the store with the largest shortage and its sales RANK: the “sales rank” column;
and the line under the table: how many of these stores are among the 20 worst by sales.
cards.note: The fourth number is the key one. If the store with the largest shortage sits mid-table by sales, then judged by sales it is easy to mistake for a weak store. The whole course was built around this trap.

cards.heading: If these numbers are not in the report
cards.code_title: Add this to the same conversation with the model
cards.text:
This happens to most people, and it is not your oversight: the report calculates exactly what you asked for in the TASK block. If sales rank or the share is missing, the task was phrased more broadly, and the report needs extending.
