This is not a rebuild from scratch and no reason to abandon the lesson: one request in the same conversation with the model, a new file, and the numbers will appear.
cards.code_text:
Add four numbers at the top: how many bottles were lost
over the period, what share of actual sales this represents,
at how many stores the product ran out before delivery, and which
store lost the most.

Below, a table of ALL such stores, sorted by lost sales, descending,
with a “sales rank” column (the store's position in the list
sorted by sales). Do not truncate the table.

Under the table, in one line: how many of these stores are among
the 20 worst by sales.

Calculate lost sales like this: take the days when sales are zero
and stock is zero, and multiply them by that store's usual daily
rate for that item.
cards.note: This will be your first revision of the report. How to publish the corrected file without losing the address and access is covered later, in the lesson “The first version is always wrong”; for now it is enough to open the new file with a double click and drag the extract into it.

cards.heading: Write down the first version's numbers
cards.text:
The field is saved in your browser and is not sent anywhere.

Write them down, and do not trust them yet. The report calculated exactly what you asked for, from whatever was in the file, and nobody has checked the file yet. The next lesson is data acceptance, then revising the report, and only after that reconciliation. That is when you will see how far the first version's numbers were from the real ones.
cards.code_text:
FIRST VERSION OF THE REPORT
Lost sales over 12 weeks: ............ btl
Share of actual sales: ............ %
Stores where the product ran out before delivery: ............
Largest shortage: ............, rank ...... of 60 by sales

(you will come back here after data acceptance and revisions)
cards.code_title: First version: write it down for comparison

checks.q: The report shows lost sales of 10.2%. What does this number mean?
options: Exactly how much the company lost over the period
How many stores were left without stock before delivery
Losses are at least this share: it is a lower bound
How far actual sales diverged from the sales plan
checks.why: Out-of-stock days are multiplied by the store's usual rate. The data knows nothing at all about how many people left without finding the product, so the honest wording is “at least”, not “exactly”.

checks.q: The store with the largest shortage ranks 33rd of 60 by sales; the other thirteen stores with shortages rank even lower. The manager proposes taking volume from the 20 worst stores by sales and giving it to the leaders. What happens?
options: Volume leaves stores where it sits unsold
Volume leaves stores that are already short of it
Sales grow: the product moves to the leaders
Nothing changes: the stores' shares stay the same
checks.why: A store with no stock sells exactly what it was delivered: it is bound to sit at the bottom of the sales ranking, however much customers ask for the product. So “take from the worst by sales” hits exactly the shortages: almost all fourteen stores with shortages fall into that bottom twenty. Stores where product really sits unsold show up not in sales but in write-offs.

takeaways: The report shows numbers; a person reads the answer off them.
It is too early to trust the first version's numbers: the file has not been checked yet.
A store's sales rank does not measure demand if the product ran out.

lessons.title: Data acceptance: check the file yourself
lessons.summary: Five checks for any extract, and the nine numbers they produce

cards.text:
From here on it is work, not reading. But before calculating anything from the file, you accept it: you ask the extract five questions, and none of them is specific to Delta. They are the same questions you would ask of any table that reaches you from someone else's system.

The numbers are deliberately not printed below. Get your own first, then answer the questions at the end of the lesson: that is where their meaning is explained. That way the findings are yours, not something you were told.

cards.heading: Five questions for any extract
cards.text: This is data acceptance. It takes ten minutes, saves you rebuilding an entire report, and is done BEFORE the calculations, not after a number fails to match.
list: completeness: are there as many rows as there should be? Multiply what the table is made of: stores × items × days;

uniqueness: each row has a key, a set of columns that does not repeat. Here it is date + store + item. Compare the row count with the number of unique keys: if they differ, the data is duplicated or the wrong key was chosen;
gaps: where are the blanks, and what does a blank mean: zero, or “the event did not happen”? These are different things, and confusing them is the costliest mistake;
units: are all rows in the same units of measure, and is there anything to check that against: a second sheet, another report, warehouse shipments;
outliers: is there a period, store or item that stands out from the rest by a multiple?
cards.note: On the platform this happens automatically: a report generator declares its checks in the manifest (key uniqueness, non-empty columns, ranges), and the Data Quality section shows the findings after every run. While the report is built by hand, these five questions are your job.

cards.heading: If you do not have the extract to hand
cards.text: Get it here: it is the same file this whole lesson is about. Next to it are the warehouse shipments (you will need them in step 5 to understand the units story) and the sample report: it reads this extract and calculates the same things, if you would rather not wrestle with formulas.
cards.note: Columns: A date · B weekday · C week · D city · E channel · F store · G item · H sales · I delivery · J write-off · K stock. The formulas below are written for these letters.

cards.heading: Nine steps in Excel
cards.code_title: Checklist: go in order, paste formulas into an empty cell
cards.text:
This is NOT a prompt for the model: you carry out these nine points by hand in your own Excel. Paste the formula from the relevant point into any empty cell next to the data (for example N1) and see what it shows; points 2 and 3 are not formulas but two menu actions.

The order follows the five acceptance questions: steps 1–4 cover completeness, uniqueness and gaps, 5–6 units, 7–9 the substantive calculation and outliers. Calculating the substance before acceptance is the most expensive way to save time.
cards.code_text:
1. Total number of rows
   =COUNTA(A:A)-1

2. Key uniqueness: is any row present twice?
   Data → Remove Duplicates, tick ONLY “date”,
   “store”, “item”: that is the row key in this file.
   Excel will tell you how many it removed and how many remain;
   if it removed anything at all, find out why before
   calculating further.
   (Make a copy of the sheet first: removal cannot be undone.)

3. What the file should consist of: in a pivot table, drag
   “store” into rows (how many?), then “item”, then “date”.
   Multiply the three numbers and compare with point 1.

4. Blank sales cells are not zeros
   =COUNTBLANK(H2:H21841)

5. Sales “as is”, with no processing at all
   =SUM(H:H)
   And by city:  =SUMIF(D:D,"Riverton",H:H)
   and the same for “Northfield” and “Lakeside”

6. Align the units. New column L, first row:
   =IF(OR(D2="Northfield",D2="Lakeside"),H2*12,H2)
   fill down, then =SUM(L:L) again

7. Days when there was nothing to sell
   =COUNTIFS(H:H,0,K:K,0)
   and how many stores that is: a pivot by “store” filtered on “sales = 0”

8. Write-offs where there was stock
   =SUMIFS(J:J,K:K,">0")   (and on column L, if you aligned the units)

9. Weekly profile: pivot “week” → sum of column L
cards.note: The Copy button takes the whole checklist: handy to keep it alongside, in a text editor or a second sheet. A single formula is easier to select with the mouse right here. And yes, each point will give you a number: write it down, as the reconciliation will be based on them.

cards.heading: The same with queries on the platform
cards.code_title: Copy one query at a time, from the “-- Query N” line to the “;”
cards.text:
If you would rather not open Excel, the platform gives you the same numbers. Explore → “Folder with files…” (a folder of .xlsx workbooks; .csv files are not read from there, so save as .xlsx) → “Refresh index from folder”. The platform recognizes a folder from a report's catalog by itself, and takes an ordinary folder as is: each table is named after its file, so delta-sales.xlsx becomes the table delta_sales. The table names are shown in the line under the button; if yours is different, replace it in the queries.

Run the queries ONE AT A TIME: take everything from the “-- Query N” line up to and including the semicolon. Half a query or a single line of one will not run: the engine accepts only a complete query starting with SELECT or WITH.
cards.code_text:
-- Query 2. Key uniqueness: the two numbers should match.
SELECT count(*) AS total,
       count(DISTINCT ("date", store, item)) AS unique_keys
FROM delta_sales;

-- Query 3. What the file consists of.
WITH u AS (SELECT * FROM delta_sales
           QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "date", store, item) = 1)
SELECT count(DISTINCT store) AS stores,
       count(DISTINCT item) AS items,
       count(DISTINCT "date") AS days
FROM u;

-- Query 5-6. Sales as is and after aligning the units.
WITH u AS (SELECT * FROM delta_sales
           QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "date", store, item) = 1)
SELECT city,
       sum(sales) AS as_is,
       sum(sales * CASE WHEN city IN ('Northfield','Lakeside') THEN 12 ELSE 1 END) AS bottles
FROM u GROUP BY city ORDER BY city;

-- Query 7. Out-of-stock days and the stores where they occurred.
WITH u AS (SELECT * FROM delta_sales
           QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "date", store, item) = 1)
SELECT count(*) AS days, count(DISTINCT store) AS stores
FROM u WHERE sales = 0 AND stock = 0;

-- Query 8. Write-offs with stock on hand.
WITH u AS (SELECT * FROM delta_sales
           QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "date", store, item) = 1)
SELECT count(DISTINCT store) AS stores,
       sum("write-off" * CASE WHEN city IN ('Northfield','Lakeside') THEN 12 ELSE 1 END) AS bottles
FROM u WHERE "write-off" > 0 AND stock > 0;

-- Query 9. Weekly profile: one week should stand out.
WITH u AS (SELECT * FROM delta_sales
           QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "date", store, item) = 1)
SELECT week,
       sum(sales * CASE WHEN city IN ('Northfield','Lakeside') THEN 12 ELSE 1 END) AS bottles
FROM u GROUP BY week ORDER BY week;
cards.note: Duplicates are removed right in the query, by the WITH u AS (…) block; in Excel you removed them in step 2. Without it the numbers will not match the reference: you would get 1,979 out-of-stock days instead of 1,826. The folder will have no metrics or Ask suggestions: metrics are declared by a report's author, and a folder has no author.

cards.heading: How to tell whether you got it right
cards.text:
Below are six questions, one per finding. Each describes what you should have seen with your own eyes; your job is to say what it means.

If a number did not match, do not guess: the lesson “Reconcile and find where it broke” is entirely about finding the point where your calculation diverged from the file.

takeaways: Nine actions on the file, and you arrive at the six findings yourself.
Check the file's integrity BEFORE calculating anything important from it.
Units are aligned before the calculation, not after: otherwise packs get added to bottles.

checks.q: Removing duplicates on “date + store + item” removed 1,680 rows out of 21,840. The file has 60 stores, 4 items and 84 days. What do these numbers tell you?
options: The file is incomplete: some days were not exported
One entire week got into the file twice
Some stores have no sales for one of the items
The repeats are random; extracts always have a few
checks.why: 60 × 4 × 84 = 20,160: that is how many rows a complete grid has, and exactly that many remained. And 1,680 = 60 × 4 × 7: an entire week, with all stores and items. Random repeats do not look like that.

checks.q: COUNTBLANK on the sales column returns 20 out of 21,840 rows. How should you read this?
options: Twenty rows got corrupted during the export
Sales were zero on twenty occasions
One store was closed for five days
Twenty stores forgot to report for a day
checks.why: 20 = 5 days × 4 items: one store was closed for refurbishment. Blank and zero are different events: blank means “not trading”, zero means “trading, but no product”. Counting blanks as zero adds a fifteenth store with shortages that does not exist.

checks.q: The sales column totals 584,977, while over the same period the warehouse shipped 1,817,738 bottles. Sales are a third of shipments. Why?
options: Two thirds of the product piled up in store stockrooms
Some of the sales did not make it into the extract
The warehouse ships with a margin to cover losses
Two cities record packs rather than bottles
checks.why: By city it is plain to see: 492,808 for Riverton against 48,999 and 43,170 for the other two, with equal shipments. 48,999 × 12 = 587,988, which matches. The conversion factor is not in the extract itself; it comes from an independent source, and the report states it explicitly.

checks.q: The condition “sales = 0 and stock = 0” yields 1,826 days across 14 stores. What are these stores?
options: Stores that ran out before the next delivery
Stores with the weakest demand in the network
Stores whose tills were down on those days
Stores closed for refurbishment or holidays
checks.why: Zero sales with zero stock does not mean “nobody bought” but “there was nothing to sell”. Such a store's sales equal what was delivered, so its demand is entirely invisible in the extract: it will stay at the bottom of the sales ranking forever.

checks.q: Weekly pivot: one week shows 230,400 btl, the other eleven range from 122,204 to 124,869. What do you do with the outlier?
options: Keep it in sales, but do not use it as the norm
Remove it from the report as an outlier
Split it in half: it looks like repeated rows
Base the norm on it: it is the most complete
checks.why: This is a promotion week: the sales are real, and they are not removed from actuals. But they are not the usual rate: if you take them as the norm, you inflate both the norm and the shortage estimate by about 7%.

checks.q: Write-offs with stock on hand total 201,151 btl across 46 stores, and none of them is among the 14 stores with shortages. What conclusion follows?
options: We need to buy more: there is not enough product
Write-offs are unavoidable; it is normal spoilage
The volume exists but sits where it is not needed
The data is contradictory: this cannot happen
checks.why: Two problems at different stores with no overlap at all: that is the signature of a distribution error, not of purchase volume. 201,151 btl of write-offs against 163,548 btl of shortage: the source of volume lies within the same purchase.

lessons.title: The first version is always wrong
lessons.summary: Build in the acceptance findings and publish a version, not a new report

cards.text:
The question is asked in front of everyone, and there is nothing to say: the report really does show that. And yet you already know the answer; you found it during acceptance: Northfield keeps its records in packs of 12 bottles, and the report added packs to bottles.

This is the normal course of events. The first version of a report is almost always wrong, not because you did a poor job, but because data reveals its quirks only once you check it. What is not normal is abandoning that version and publishing a new report next to it.

cast.say: Why are Northfield's sales twelve times lower than Riverton's?

cards.heading: Fix it in the same conversation with the model
cards.text:
The four revisions below are the four acceptance findings translated into a request. Do not describe the task again: add them to the same conversation in which the report was born.

Note what they do not contain: a single value from your file. No city names, no store codes, no items. The model receives the RULE, and you fill in the specific values yourself, in the file, on your own machine.
cards.code_text:
Units of measure differ by the value in the “city” column: some are
units, some are packs. Do not ask me which ones, and do not expect
names: put it in a setting at the top of the file:

  // I will fill this in myself; it is not sent anywhere
  var PACKS = { /* "value from the city column": units per pack */ };

and convert sales to units using this table BEFORE any calculation.

One week in the file may be duplicated: its rows repeat.
Drop repeats by the key date + store + item.

Do not use a week that stands out from the rest by almost double as
the usual sales rate: exclude it from the norm calculation, but keep
it in actual sales. Put the number of that week in a setting next to
PACKS as well; I will fill it in myself.

A blank sales cell means “the store was not trading”, not zero.
Do not count such days as out-of-stock days.
cards.note: The field is editable and saved in your browser. Replace the city and column names with your own when you fix a real report.
cards.code_title: Add this to the same conversation with the model

cards.heading: Why the revisions contain no names
cards.text:
A course rule that, for the first time, starts to matter in money terms: what goes out is STRUCTURE and RULES, never values. Column names, the format of records, the calculation logic: yes. Customer names, store codes, tax IDs, people's names: no.

In the training file the “city” column holds harmless made-up names. In your real file it will hold customers, retail chains or people, and a conversation with an external model is not the place for them to appear. The report loses nothing: the rule “units differ; here is the setting” works exactly the same way.
list: the rule goes into the prompt: “units in this column differ; convert to units”;
the values go into the file: a settings line you fill in on your own machine;
the check is by eye: open the finished file and make sure the model has not baked in a single one of your values.
cards.note: The sample report in this course is built the same way: the pack factors sit on a separate line at the top of the file, neither derived from the data nor obtained from the conversation.

cards.heading: And if real values are unavoidable
cards.text: This is not a rare case but everyday work: half the rules in real data hinge on specific names of customers, chains or legal entities. Work down the list from the top: take the first option that covers your task.

head: What you need
What to do
rows: The value is needed only by the calculation (a factor, rate or threshold)
A setting at the top of the file: the model leaves an empty line, and you fill in the values on your own machine
The model needs a sample record: what your rows look like

Run the extract through Anonymizer; the six illustrated steps are covered in the lesson “Anonymize an extract in five minutes”. It returns a file with the same record format and, at the bottom, a ready-made sample: the header and three anonymized rows, which are what goes into the prompt
You need a mapping: code → name, customer → chain
A reference table on the platform: the report reads it itself at run time, and only the column name goes into the conversation
You need to calculate something on the values themselves
The Explore tab: the question becomes SQL, calculated by your browser or the platform's server. The model receives table and column names, never cells
You can neither anonymize nor calculate on your own side
This is not a task for an external model. Such tasks are rare, but they exist, and admitting it is cheaper than explaining yourself later

cards.note: Anonymizer itself finds names, tax IDs, social security numbers, passports, phone numbers and email addresses, and replaces them while keeping the shape of the record: length, format, separators. Codes like “RV-01” remain codes, the same value is masked identically across the whole workbook, and numbers and dates are left alone, so the anonymized file gives the same totals. Before it starts, it inspects the workbook and warns you about what would travel with it: hidden sheets, lookup tables in named ranges, links to other files, comments and the author's name in the properties. Afterwards it honestly lists the columns you left as they were. The page runs entirely in the browser and is locked down so that it physically cannot make a network request.

cards.heading: Where to put the corrected file
cards.text:
Open your report, expand the panel on the right and go to the Versions tab. At the top is the “New version” section: choose the corrected file and click “Upload new version”. The version number goes up; the address and access stay the same: the link you have already sent out will show the corrected report.

Further down the same tab is the history: every previous version has a “Restore” button.
cards.note: Data is changed elsewhere, on the Data tab. The rule is simple: if the calculation or the look of the report has changed, it is a version; if a new extract has arrived, it is data.

cards.heading: How many times to repeat this
cards.text:
Usually two or three rounds. The sign that it is time to stop is not “it looks nice now” but “the numbers have stopped changing with revisions”: you fixed one more small thing, and the four headline numbers stayed the same. That means the answer is stable.

The opposite sign exists too: if every revision moves the headline number by tens of percent, you do not have an answer yet. You have a draft, and it is too early to show it.
cards.note: Versions are cheap and reversible: every previous one has a “Restore” button, and the restore itself becomes a new version too. Publishing is not risky; silently leaving a wrong version up is.

checks.q: You have fixed the calculation in the report. Where do you put the new file?
options: Versions tab, “New version” section
Data tab, “Upload slots” next to the file
The Upload page: upload the report again
Settings tab, the report title field
checks.why: Data and the report itself live in different places. A new calculation is a version: the address and access are preserved, and the link you sent out immediately shows the corrected report.

checks.q: After the third revision the headline number moved by 0.3%. What does that tell you?
options: The calculation is broken: numbers must match exactly
The revisions achieved nothing; a different approach is needed
Time to present: the answer is stable under revisions
Keep going until the number stops changing entirely
checks.why: Stability under small revisions is precisely the sign of a finished answer. Waiting for the number to stop moving altogether is pointless: a lower-bound estimate does not need to be accurate to the bottle.

checks.q: In your extract, units of measure depend on the customer's legal entity, and legal entity names must not be shared externally. What do you do?
options: Give the model the entity names, or it won't understand
Drop the revision: the calculation is impossible without names
Ask for a setting in the file and fill in the names yourself
Replace names with numbers and explain them in the chat
checks.why: The model needs the rule, not the values: “units depend on the value in this column; put the mapping table in a setting”. You fill in the names in the file on your own machine. Replacing them with numbers and decoding them in the conversation is the same leak, just in two steps.

task.text: Publish the second version of your report: open it, go to the panel on the right, Versions tab → “Upload new version”.
task.hint: I can't see a report that you own with a version above 1 yet. Upload the corrected file on the Versions tab and come back.

takeaways: The first version of a report is almost always wrong: data reveals itself only when checked.
Rules and structure go into the prompt; values stay in your file.
Data is changed on the Data tab, the report itself on the Versions tab.

lessons.title: Reconcile and find where it broke
lessons.summary: The corrected report's numbers against the reference, and a ladder for when they don't match

cards.text: The file has been accepted, the findings built in, the report recalculated and published as version two: now a comparison makes sense. Before, there was nothing to compare: the first version worked from an unchecked file and could match the reference only by chance.

head: What we calculate
Reference
rows: Rows in the file · unique keys (date + store + item)
Sales as is · after aligning units
Out-of-stock days · at how many stores
RV-02: 19,657 btl, rank 33 of 60 by sales

cards.heading: What changed after the revisions
cards.code_title: Copy the second version's numbers here
cards.text: Go back to the numbers you wrote down at the start of this unit and put the new ones next to them. The difference between the columns is the value of data acceptance, and it is worth seeing with your own eyes: it is usually tens of percent, and for sales it can be a multiple.
cards.code_text:
first version   after revisions   reference
Lost sales, btl         ............    ............      163,548
Share of sales, %       ............    ............      10.2
Stores with shortages   ............    ............      14
Actual sales            ............    ............      1,598,836
cards.note: If the second column matches the third, excellent. If not, but all the acceptance control numbers matched, the difference lies in the assumptions, and the next lesson is about exactly that.

cards.heading: Not matching is a working situation, not your failure
cards.text:
An experienced analyst's first calculation does not match either. The only difference is that they do not start over or fudge the answer; they find the break point: they go through the control numbers from top to bottom until they hit the first mismatch. Reconciling beyond that is pointless: everything below was calculated on a broken foundation.

The next screen is exactly such a ladder: the control numbers in order, and next to each, what a mismatch means. Work down it strictly from the top.
cards.note: A calculation error is nothing to be ashamed of. What is shameful is presenting a number in a meeting without knowing where it came from.

cards.heading: Where exactly it broke
cards.text: The first mismatch from the top is your break point. Fix it and recalculate: the other discrepancies usually disappear by themselves.

head: If this does not match
It means this
rows: The file was not read in full: Excel stopped at the first empty row, or a filter was left on
Duplicates were checked across the whole row instead of the three columns together, and then they are not repeats
Only one of the two sheets was read, or some rows were hidden by a filter
Blanks were replaced with zeros on import: go back to the original file
Numbers were read as text: a decimal comma and a space as the thousands separator
The factor of 12 was applied to the wrong cities, or applied twice
The condition kept only zero sales, without zero stock
Check the assumptions: the promotion week and the duplicated week (the next lesson covers this)

cards.heading: A discrepancy within the assumptions is not an error
cards.text:
If you got 9.4% instead of 10.2% and all eight control numbers matched, that is not an error but a different definition of a “usual day”. Three reasonable definitions give three different numbers, and all three are honest as long as the assumption is stated out loud.

That is why the conclusion reads “we are losing at least 10.2% under these assumptions” rather than “we are losing 10.2%”. The next lesson shows the full range.
cards.note: A simple rule: a discrepancy within 10–15% means different assumptions; a discrepancy by a multiple means a break, which you find using the ladder of control numbers.

cards.heading: Why stores with shortages are invisible in sales
cards.text: One observation that made all this calculation worthwhile. The fourteen stores with shortages rank from 33rd to 60th by sales: none in the top half, eleven in the bottom twenty. The store with the largest shortage, RV-02, ranks 33rd: solidly mid-table.
list: the decision to “take volume from the 20 worst by sales” would hit 11 of the 14;
whereas all twenty top stores by sales have write-offs.
cards.note: A store with no stock sells exactly what it was delivered, so it is bound to look weak, however much customers ask for the product. You can only see this through stock, and no sales ranking will ever show it.

cards.heading: If it really did not work out
cards.text:
It happens: the file would not open, the formulas produced nonsense, there is no time. That is no reason to abandon the course halfway: take the ready-made version and complete the rest with it.

The sample report reads the same extract and prints the four headline numbers itself: just drag the file into it. This is a legitimate path: your goal in this course is to learn to ask questions of data and defend the answer, not to compete on speed with formulas.
cards.note: Still, come back to the nine steps when you have half an hour. The difference between “I was told” and “I saw it myself” is audible in a meeting straight away.

checks.q: You have 177,000 in lost sales at a share of 10.3%. The share is almost the same as the reference. What does this mean?
options: No error: the share matches, so everything is right
A duplicated week inflated sales and the shortage
A different assumption about the store's usual rate
The file turned out to contain more than 60 stores
checks.why: A copy of a week raises the numerator and the denominator at once, so the share looks healthy while the absolute number is off by almost 14,000 bottles. Reconciling percentages alone is not enough.

checks.q: Your number is 9.4%, the reference is 10.2%. What is the right course of action?
options: Adjust the calculation to hit the reference 10.2%
Put both numbers in the report and not choose between them
State your assumption and keep your own answer
Round to 10%: the difference is immaterial
checks.why: It is not the answers that differ but the assumptions about which days count as usual. A stated assumption makes the number defensible; fitting it to someone else's result robs you of understanding where it came from.

takeaways: Reconcile from top to bottom and stop at the first mismatch: that is the break point.
A discrepancy within the assumptions is not an error; a discrepancy by a multiple is a broken foundation.
A store with no stock is bound to look weak in any sales ranking.

lessons.title: The answer is a range, not a number
lessons.summary: Four assumptions, four numbers, and one that cannot be met

cards.text: Until now, the wording “we are losing at least 10.2% under these assumptions” has sounded like a polite caveat. Time to name those assumptions one by one: there are four, all about the same thing, namely what counts as a store's usual rate. And all four can be checked in ten minutes on the same extract.

cards.heading: The same data, four answers
cards.text: Below are the results on our extract. There is no error in any row: only the definition of a “usual day” changes.

head: What counts as the usual rate
Answer
rows: Average over days with stock, promotion week excluded
The same, but with the promotion week included

cards.heading: What each row means
cards.text:
The first is our choice, and you need to be able to name it. The second is the cost of a single mistake: the promotion week is 1.85 times higher than usual, so it raises the norm and, with it, the shortage by 7%.

The third row is not an alternative answer but a check. The median is insensitive to outliers; if the answer barely changes with it (163,295 against 163,548, a difference of 0.2%), then the result does not hinge on a couple of odd days but reflects a stable pattern. Two minutes of work, and half the questions in the meeting are dealt with in advance.
cards.note: “I checked it with the median, and the conclusion holds” is a sentence after which people argue with the decision, not with your arithmetic. Those are different conversations, and the second is more useful.

cards.heading: The fourth row is the most useful
cards.text:
“Calculate the rate from the days before delivery; they are the most telling” sounds reasonable, yet the answer drops to zero. The reason is simple: a store that runs out has, by definition, no stock in the days before delivery; that is exactly when it stands empty. The assumption cannot be met on precisely the rows it was introduced for.

Hence a rule worth more than the case itself: an assumption is tested not on the whole table but on the rows you intend to apply it to.

cast.say: It came out as zero not because there are no losses, but because there was nothing to calculate from.

takeaways: An honest analysis has not one number but a range with stated assumptions.
Swapping the average for the median is a two-minute check of how robust the conclusion is.
An assumption is tested on the rows it was introduced for.

checks.q: Switching from the average to the median moved the answer by 0.2%. What does that tell you?
options: The median is calculated incorrectly in this task
There is too little data to see a difference
The average and median always coincide here
The conclusion does not rest on a few odd days
checks.why: The median is insensitive to outliers. Two estimates agreeing means the pattern is stable, and that is a strong argument to have before anyone asks for it.

checks.q: The assumption “calculate the rate from the days before delivery” gives zero. What does that mean?
options: There are no losses: the calculation shows it directly
No basis: stores with shortages have no such days
The extract is missing the days before delivery
Zero is an ordinary division error in the calculation
checks.why: A store with a stockout has no stock in the days before delivery: that is when it stands empty. The assumption turned out to be impossible to meet exactly where it was meant to be applied.

lessons.title: From a number to a recommendation
lessons.summary: What to write to your manager so that something changes on Monday

cards.text:
163,548 bottles is not yet a recommendation. A recommendation answers the question “what do we do on Monday”, and it has an addressee.

The other half of the answer is in the same extract: at 46 stores product is written off while stock is on hand, 201,151 bottles over 12 weeks, 12.6% of sales. These 46 never overlap with the fourteen, and they include ALL TWENTY of the top stores by sales. The company has the volume; it sits at the strong stores and never reaches the ones that are short. There is no need to buy more; it needs to be moved.

cards.heading: A five-line email
cards.text: Every line here is mandatory, and the order is deliberate: the decision, the facts, what the data does not contain, the proposal, the assumptions and how to prove yourself wrong. Remove any one of them, and the email turns into a progress report.
cards.code_text:
Decision: how to allocate the weekly delivery across stores.

What the data shows: 14 stores consistently run out of stock 2-3 days
  before delivery; we are losing at least 163,548 btl, 10.2% of sales.
  At the other 46 stores, 201,151 btl were written off over the same period.

What the data does not show: demand. A store with no stock sells exactly
  what it was delivered, so judged by sales it looks weak.

Proposal: move volume from stores with write-offs to stores with shortages,
  starting with RV-02, and review the result after 4 weeks.

Assumptions: the usual rate is based on days with stock; the promotion week
  and the duplicated week are excluded; this is a lower-bound estimate.

What would prove me wrong: if write-offs rise at the stores with shortages
  after they receive more volume, the problem was not the shortage.
cards.code_title: Email template: adapt it to your case

cards.heading: What the email must not contain
cards.text: Three phrases that destroy trust in an analysis faster than any arithmetic error.
list: “Losses amounted to exactly 163,548 bottles”: it is a lower-bound estimate, so say so;
“Take volume from the stores with lower sales”: those are precisely the stores where the product runs out;
“Sales will grow by N%”: you have no demand data, so there is nothing to base a growth promise on.
cards.note: The last line of the email is not a courtesy. An analyst who states in advance what would prove them wrong gets a discussion of substance; an analyst who defends a number gets an argument about the number.

cards.text:
Notice how the conversation ended: not with praise for the report, but with a decision and the date of the next review. That is what an analyst's work produces: not a file, but a decision someone has made, and a way to find out a month later whether it was right.

The report has not gone anywhere: it sits at its address, is updated on Tuesdays, and a month from now will answer the same question with new numbers.

cast.say: Fine. We'll start with RV-02, and in a month you'll show me the same report.

checks.q: The analysis found 163,548 btl of lost sales, 10.2% of actuals; the store's usual rate is based on days with stock. Which sentence do you write to your manager?
options: “Losses are 163,548 bottles; this is the exact figure”
“If we unload the weak stores, sales will grow”
“We lose at least 10.2%: rate based on days with stock”
“There is nothing to calculate without demand data”
checks.why: Exactly two things are defensible: a number qualified with “at least” and the stated assumption it was derived from. The exact size of the losses is simply not in the data, since demand is not recorded there; nobody promised sales growth; and “unload the weak stores” is the very decision that would hit the stores with shortages.

checks.q: A month has passed: the volume was moved, and write-offs rose at the stores that received more. What does this mean for your recommendation?
options: The recommendation is confirmed: the product finally arrived
The disproof triggered: the problem was not the shortage
Write-offs and volume allocation are unrelated to each other
These stores need even more volume, and then we wait
checks.why: This is exactly the signal you named in the email in advance: the product was delivered but not bought, so the demand was not there, and the shortage was not the cause. That is what the “what would prove me wrong” line is for: a month later it shows whether the decision worked, and there is no need to argue about it.

takeaways: A number becomes a recommendation when the decision, the assumptions and a way to prove yourself wrong are stated.
A lower-bound estimate is written as exactly that: “at least”, not “exactly”.
An analyst's output is a decision taken and a review date, not a file.

lessons.title: What next
lessons.summary: Where to go when you want more

cards.heading: What you can now do
cards.text: An hour ago you had someone else's complaint: “either the shelves are empty or we're writing stock off”. Now you have a number you can defend and a decision that can be checked in a month. Along the way you learned eight things, and none of them is about OnePage buttons:
list: turning a complaint into a question that has a decision, a deadline and a constraint;
breaking a problem into branches that do not overlap, including the “the data is wrong” branch;
stating a hypothesis before opening the file, and saying in advance what would kill it;
seeing what the data does not contain: demand, units of measure, the reason for a blank cell;
catching six common extract failures: stockouts, write-offs, packs, duplicates, promotions, blanks;
testing a conclusion for robustness and honestly naming assumptions instead of one pretty number;
taking a report through to a second version rather than abandoning the first;
writing five lines that lead to someone making a decision.
cards.note: The eighth point is the only one the other seven exist for. A report nobody read and an analysis after which nothing changed are worth the same: nothing.

cards.text:
A month has passed. Every Tuesday by lunchtime, people at the company open the same report: first the manager, then the warehouse, then the area managers. Nobody asks for it to be sent; everyone knows the address.

That is the result: not a beautiful file, but a habit. You can build a report, check it, publish it, update it and keep it from getting lost. None of these steps was difficult on its own; the hard part was getting started.

cast.say: It's Tuesday. Where's the report?

cards.heading: If you want to go further
cards.text: Three paths, and they all start here. None is mandatory: the Tuesday report works without them. Choose based on what is getting in your way right now.
list: The core course, Working on the platform: how the platform works inside and why it is built that way.
Dev Guide: a short reference on prompts, formats and frequently asked questions.
Generators: for when the same report is needed every week and you are tired of building it by hand.

cards.text:
And the most useful thing of all: show your first report to a colleague. Five minutes of feedback are worth two hours of polishing.

A report that gets opened every week becomes a habit within a month; a report that has been forgotten cannot be saved by any amount of polish. A week from now, ask your colleague whether they opened your report: the answer will tell you more about it than any polishing.
cards.note: Your second report will come more easily: take the ready-made prompt from the course and change the same two lines in it.

checks.q: The store report is needed every Tuesday on new data. What do you choose?
options: Ask the model to rebuild it from scratch every week
Copy last week's report and edit the numbers
Build a generator: it will rebuild the report itself
Calculate in a spreadsheet and publish by hand
checks.why: A generator means the calculation is described once and repeated at the click of a button on new files. The core course covers it; asking the model to redo everything every time produces a slightly different report each time.

takeaways: The outcome of the course is not a file but a habit: question → data → assumptions → decision.
A report stays alive as long as people open it: an address, an update schedule and one owner.
Show your first report to a colleague: five minutes of feedback cost less than two hours of polishing.
